title: Identity and composition of arbitrary logarithmic morphisms
statement: For arbitrary schemes with etale log structures and relative-section log morphisms [def-trf-log-ideal-chart-presentation], there are identity log maps $1_M$ and composites $g\circ f$. The base of a composite is the composite of scheme maps. On every compatible relative etale triangle its section map is the composite of the two given section maps. These triangle equations determine the composite uniquely. Identities fix every relative section; composition satisfies both identity laws and associativity. These constructions specialize to fs locally Noetherian objects [def-trf-fs-log-blowup], whose identity satisfies the prescribed identity condition [def-per-strict-log-morphism]. Strict etale log maps, meaning bijective canonical restriction maps on every relative etale test object, compose.

source.place: VI 1.1, p.69 (log-morphism conventions); VIII 3.3.4(ii), p.107. Explicit relative-section construction written by F3; Kato 1988 section 1.

proof.text: For a relative diagram V to W over a composite, pull W back along the second map. The lift of V to this etale intermediate test object exists by the scheme product property. Compose the two section maps. Naturality and compatibility with regular functions follow from naturality of the given maps and the two projection equations.

For any other intermediate etale test triangle, its map to the canonical pullback and naturality identify the section-map composites. Conversely the triangle using the canonical pullback determines the composite, including its base.

The identity uses the restriction homomorphisms on the etale site. Naturality gives its triangle equations. Uniqueness of the composite proves both identity laws. For associativity, use two successive canonical pullbacks and apply the triangle equations to the same three section maps. For strict etale composition, those equations express the canonical restriction map as the composite of two bijections; ordinary etale composition supplies the base condition.
